tasks.title: Discover and turn on the Content Variants feature
tasks.titleRaw: Task 1 · Discover and turn on the Content Variants feature
tasks.intro: A team that keeps hand-building personalized content finds out what Content Variants does for them, and switches it on.
tasks.desiredExperience: The team evaluates and adopts Content Variants with low risk. It's clear enough to judge fit quickly and cheap enough to try before committing budget, so they start their first project with confidence instead of guesswork.

flows.title: Discover > Try out > Upgrade

phases.title: Pay

phases.title: Turn it on
phases.description: A developer enables the feature; editors see the perspective bar’s second row appear.

flows.success: The team can say what Content Variants does for them, and it is actively available both within Studio and while querying Content Lake. The content editor was able to try out the feature non-destructively.
flows.failure: They cannot tell whether it beats building it themselves, or whether it fits how they already work. Content editors are not able to find or use the feature, and revert back to creating duplicate documents.

painPoints.text: The content editor rearranges homepage content by hand.

quote.quote: “Just on the home page is a massive manual lift of very little change… all I can do is just shuffle stuff,”

painPoints.text: Manual personalization leads to a lot of duplicate documents.
Studio is perceived as complex and understanding when to use variant documents vs. document copies, and how to set them up is complicated.
Existing plugins like the localization plugin compete for certain use cases.
Adoption risk: Releases have been priced too expensively and prohibited customers from trying out the feature.
Documentation and set up may be complicated if external systems need to be hooked up.
A first look shows what the feature does, not how it fits the team’s own content and way of working.

quote.quote: “I feel like this is a tool that will work. I don’t know if we’re going to be able to use it,”

flows.title: Hit a limit, upgrade

phases.title: Hit the limit and upgrade
phases.description: A developer already on the free tier hits the plan’s cap on variant definitions and is offered a path to upgrade.

flows.trigger: A developer is using Content Variants for free and keeps adding variant definitions beyond the free limit as the team’s needs grow.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: The developer creates one more variant definition and hits the free plan’s limit.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They see a small block explaining the limit and the advantages of the full feature-set of Variants on Enterprise plans, leading to an action to upgrade.

flows.success: The team upgrades the plan and continues adding variant definitions, while leveraging the ability to create more than one dimension to personalize their content.
flows.failure: The team stays on the limit, and either works around it or puts further definitions on hold.

tasks.title: Configure variant definitions
tasks.intro: A developer decides where the definitions come from and how they are referenced in Sanity; a content editor changes, organises and uses them.
tasks.desiredExperience: Setting up variant definitions feels like configuration, not decoding. Teams reuse the audience and dimension logic they already trust from their source-of-truth systems, using names they recognize instead of cryptic flag IDs, so defining a new variant takes minutes, not a support ticket.

flows.title: A developer decides where the source data for variant definitions come from and hooks them up

phases.title: Choose the source
phases.description: Decide where the source data for variant definitions come from, and for which dataset.

phases.title: Verify
phases.description: See the variant definitions appear in the perspective bar.

flows.trigger: The developer needs to set up Content Variants, or change where the source of the data for variant definitions come from.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They choose the source: the CDP, other experimentation platform, a hard-coded list, a Sanity document, a spreadsheet or any other endpoint where their source of truth lives.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They decide which dataset the definitions land in.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: If the source can push, they wire the push, a webhook or a function.

steps.label: STEP 4
steps.text: They open a document and check that the definitions appear in the perspective selector and in the variants tool
steps.surface: perspective selector variants overview, variant definition detail screen
surfaces: perspective selector variants overview, variant definition detail screen
steps.screenCaption: Variant definitions overview, with the perspective bar's Version and Variant dropdowns above it.

flows.success: Definitions arrive from the chosen source, in the right dataset, and conditions validate against it.
flows.failure: No source is configured, so editors type free-text key–values; or definitions land in the wrong dataset.

painPoints.text: They cannot tell whether the audiences in Sanity are the same ones their CDP knows.
Flags defined in the CDP have to be recreated here, and their descriptions are cryptic.
The ability to import flag definitions from outside is critical for customers who already run experimentation and localization from different engines.
Each external system that supplies variant definitions adds another place where they can fail.

quote.quote: “Dependent on that integration… multiple points of failure,”

flows.failure: They name and define an audience that, worded slightly differently, another definition already covers, and neither the name nor the list makes the overlap obvious.

With a CDP connected, it is unclear whether a definition made by hand stays in sync, or which copy is the source of truth.
Who may create or lock a shared key like language, versus an ad-hoc experiment name, is not governed.

steps.text: They open the dimension map and see each dimension, the keys it owns, where its definitions come from, and how many definitions it holds.

steps.text: They look up a key and see the one dimension that owns it.

flows.title: An editor checks coverage across one dimension

phases.title: Check readiness
phases.description: See which values are covered in this release, and which are missing.

phases.title: Act on a gap
phases.description: Author it, or hold the document back.

flows.trigger: Before a release goes live, the editor needs to know whether every document in it has the variant document it needs for a dimension, for example, that everything due to publish is fully translated.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They open the release and choose the dimension to check.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They see, for just the documents in this release, which values are covered and which are missing.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They act on a gap before it ships. They author the missing variant document, or hold the document back.

flows.success: The release ships fully covered for that dimension, or the editor knowingly ships a named gap.
flows.failure: A release ships with a gap nobody caught. A document missing its French translation goes out untranslated, and the team only finds out once a customer notices.

painPoints.text: Language coverage is uneven, and nothing shows which documents still lack a variant document for a given locale.

quote.quote: “Some are in five languages, some are in two languages, some is only in one language,”

flows.title: An editor checks which conditions already belong to a definition

phases.title: Check ownership
phases.description: See who already owns a condition, and where its value comes from.

phases.title: Decide
phases.description: Reuse it, or pick something that is not already claimed.

flows.trigger: Before adding a condition, a new key or a new value for an existing key, someone needs to know whether it is already claimed by another definition, since a dimension owns its conditions exclusively.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They look up the condition key or value they are about to use.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They see which definition and dimension already own it, and where its value comes from (CDP, spreadsheet, a Sanity document, or typed by hand).

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They reuse the existing definition if it is the same dimension, or choose a different key or value. A claimed condition cannot be split across two definitions of different dimensions.
steps.screenCaption: The variant definition dialog, with one condition added.

flows.success: The new condition never collides with one that already exists elsewhere; ownership is exclusive by construction.
flows.failure: The same condition ends up claimed by two definitions without anyone noticing. Targeting turns ambiguous, and by the time it's caught, nothing points back to why.

tasks.title: Create a variant document
tasks.intro: A content editor creates a personalized variant document from a document that already exists. They start from the document, from the variant definitions overview screen, or by asking the Content Agent.
tasks.desiredExperience: Creating a variant document feels safe and fast. Editors personalize one field or a whole document without ever risking the default, see exactly what differs from the base or across versions, and never wonder whether they've overwritten something that should have stayed in sync.

phases.description: Change what should differ and tell it apart from the default.

painPoints.text: Personalized content lives in code, so editors cannot change it without a developer.

quote.quote: “If I want to change this content, I have to go through a developer,”

painPoints.text: With many audiences the list of definitions gets long to scan.
Teams that have not adopted releases meet them here for the first time.
Nothing says the variant document already existed.
Switching into one variant document hides the rest, and nothing shows the way back.

quote.quote: “I’m not even sure how to go back to seeing everything,”

painPoints.text: Across many fields: in testing, 10 of 15 editors could not complete it, citing default-state visibility, variant counts, save feedback and add/remove wording.
Field-level personalization makes the schema noisy at scale.

quote.quote: “Schema ends up being quite noisy,”

flows.title: From the Content Agent

phases.description: Say what should differ, and for which documents.

phases.description: Check each proposed variant document before it is written.

flows.trigger: The content editor wants variant documents for one audience across many documents, and does not want to create each one by hand.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They describe their intent to personalize in plain language: the audience, the documents, and what should differ.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They confirm which documents the operation covers.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: The agent proposes the variant documents as proposed changes. They preview the plan before anything is written.

steps.label: STEP 4
steps.text: They review each proposed variant document’s differences from the base document and approve, reject or re-commission them one by one.

steps.label: STEP 5
steps.text: The approved variant documents are created as drafts or into a release, and appear in each document’s version inventory.
steps.screenCaption: The document's version inventory, opened from the footer.

flows.success: Variant documents exist across the whole set for that audience, and the editor reviewed every one before it was written.
flows.failure: The agent does not know which audiences exist, or the changes land without anyone reviewing them.

painPoints.text: Personalizing many documents by hand is slow, so teams shuffle what exists rather than tailor it.

quote.quote: “Just on the home page is a massive manual lift of very little change… all I can do is just shuffle stuff,”

painPoints.text: The volume of content outgrows manual personalization, and teams want an agent that knows their audiences to decide for them.

quote.quote: “The vision would be having an autonomous agent… what’s the best next thing for that member,”

painPoints.text: The agent needs to know which audiences exist; otherwise they cannot tell whether it made the audiences up.
Without explicit control settings over the agent, teams cannot win internal approval to use it.

quote.quote: “I will never get this through if I don’t offer any control,”

tasks.title: View variant documents
tasks.intro: A content editor finds out what variant documents exist for a document, for an audience, or as a given visitor would see them, and what is live, stale or missing.
tasks.desiredExperience: Editors always know where they stand. They can name what exists, what's live, what's stale and what's missing at a glance, confidently, whether they're inside or outside the Studio, and never have to guess or double-check.

flows.title: From the document

phases.title: Take stock of the set
phases.description: Know what exists for this document, what is live, what is stale and what is missing.

flows.trigger: The editor is working in a document and needs to know what other versions or variant documents exist for it, and which do not.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They open the version inventory or the perspective bar.
steps.screenCaption: Manage versions, opened from the document footer.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They see which variant documents and release versions the current document has: one row per version, one column per dimension.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They follow one variant document across the releases it appears in.

steps.label: STEP 4
steps.text: They work out which variant documents have no published version or which version has no variant documents yet

steps.label: STEP 5 · IDEA
steps.text: They read what wins for a visitor. Rows sort by specificity (filled cells), ties break by priority, then created date, then name, and the row that wins is marked.

flows.success: They can name what exists, what is stale, and which variant documents have nothing published without opening any of them.
flows.failure: They get confused about which variant documents exist for a given dimension or release.

painPoints.text: The variant counts and the wording of the default state confuse the content editor about what exists.

quote.quote: “Returning visitors says four variants… confused,”

painPoints.text: One variant document appears once per release section it occupies; they join the rows by memory.
No way to see which stored variant document actually resolves for a given audience right now.
A coarse and a fine definition can tie, so the older one wins silently.

flows.title: Composing a perspective

phases.title: Compose a visitor
phases.description: State who you are looking as.

phases.title: Read as that visitor
phases.description: See the content the way that visitor gets it.

steps.label: STEP 2

flows.success: They can tell at a glance which visitor they are looking as.
flows.failure: The bar reads as independent pickers with no sense of a composed context.

painPoints.text: No single control shows the site as one specific visitor, such as a returning visitor in Germany.
Combining selectors narrows the view to one visitor, and nothing shows the way back to everything.

quote.quote: “I’m not even sure how to go back to seeing everything,”

Editing one audience at a time does not scale when a team runs many regional audiences.

quote.quote: “For us we’d need at least 10 audiences,”

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They see the canvas re-render live, with that version or variant applied.

flows.title: Saving a perspective as a preset

phases.title: Compose a visitor
phases.description: Assemble the combination once.

phases.title: Keep it
phases.description: Save it and pick it next time.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They assemble it once and save it as a preset.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They save the preset with a name, for themselves or for the team scope.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: Next time they pick the preset instead of rebuilding it from scratch.

flows.success: A frequent target’s perspective is one click away.
flows.failure: It takes too long to compose a desired perspective every day.

painPoints.text: They check the same combination every day and have to rebuild it each time.

flows.title: Understanding which version and variant win

phases.title: Read what wins
phases.description: Know which version this visitor is served, on what grounds, and what falls back to default.

flows.trigger: Several versions match the visitor, and they cannot tell which one the visitor actually gets.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They see every version that matches the visitor.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They see how specific each one is, and the tie-breakers in order: priority, then creation date, then name.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They see which documents match nothing and fall back to the default.

flows.success: They can state which version a visitor gets, and why.
flows.failure: They assume a specific version is what gets served, but a different one wins without them knowing.

painPoints.text: A coarse and a fine definition can tie, so the older one wins silently.

tasks.title: Review variant documents
tasks.intro: Before a variant document goes live, the editor or someone who is not the author checks what the audience will see, sees what changed, and signs it off.
tasks.desiredExperience: Reviewing feels conclusive, not provisional. The reviewer previews the page exactly as one audience will see it, sees precisely what changed against the default, and can approve in one pass, confident there's nothing left to catch later.

flows.title: Compare two versions

phases.title: Understand the differences
phases.description: Know how two versions of this document actually differ before acting on either.

flows.trigger: Two or more versions of a document exist and the reviewer must know how they differ.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They select two or more versions in the inventory.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: The full inventory opens with those versions side by side; they choose which is the base.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They read the differences field by field and act from there.

flows.success: Differences are legible without opening both documents.
flows.failure: They can’t see the two versions side by side, so they flip between two open browser tabs comparing field by field, and a small but real difference goes unnoticed.

painPoints.text: They cannot see how this version differs from the default before they ship it.
Select more to compare appears and leads nowhere.

flows.title: Preview as an audience

phases.title: Preview as an audience
phases.description: See the page the way one audience will see it.

flows.trigger: The editor wants to see the page the way one audience will see it before shipping.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They pick the audience in the perspective selector.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They open the document, or the presentation preview, and read it as that audience.
steps.screenCaption: Previewing the page as the selected audience.

flows.success: They trust that what they see is what that audience gets.
flows.failure: They preview as one audience, ship trusting it’s what that audience will see, and only learn afterward, from a customer rather than the preview, that a different segment was actually served.

painPoints.text: Reviewers cannot see a page as a given audience would, so approving a variant means signing off on something unseen.

quote.quote: “Really need in preview a way of selecting which audience,”

painPoints.text: Audience preview depends on the website’s own preview setup, which many teams do not have.

quote.quote: “We don’t have preview set up on our website,”

painPoints.text: Teams check each audience in a spreadsheet outside the Studio, a loop that audience preview in presentation could replace.

quote.quote: “Would probably replace their usage of the website for QA,”

flows.title: Get approval

phases.title: Approve
phases.description: Someone other than the author signs the change off.

flows.trigger: Someone other than the author has to sign the change off.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: The editor shows the reviewer what changed for the audience.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: The reviewer approves, or sends it back, in place.

flows.success: Approved without a back-and-forth.
flows.failure: The reviewer can’t see what actually changed for the audience from inside the Studio, so they ask the editor to explain it again over chat, and sign-off drags across several rounds.

painPoints.text: Sign-off sits with another team, and nothing packages a change so they can see and approve it quickly.

quote.quote: “Content design will be the final reviewers before something goes live,”

painPoints.text: No fast way to show a stakeholder exactly what a variant document change did.
Each change passes brand, medical and legal review, so content for each market takes longer to ship.

quote.quote: “Lots of checkpoints… brand, medical, legal,”

tasks.title: Delete a variant document
tasks.intro: A content editor removes a variant document without silently changing what an audience sees.
tasks.desiredExperience: Deleting feels confident. Editors see whose experience changes and what it changes to before they confirm, so cleanup never carries the fear of silently breaking something downstream.

flows.title: Delete a variant document from the document editor

phases.title: Decide what to retire
phases.description: Open the inventory and choose what goes.

phases.title: Confirm
phases.description: Confirm the removal.

flows.trigger: A content editor is reviewing a variant document in the editor and wants to remove one or many.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They open the inventory.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They select the variant documents to remove, and hit delete. They are able to choose a variant document in a particular version, across all versions, or narrow down the selection to a particular dimension.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They confirm in the dialog, which checks what other documents link to what’s being removed.   A variant document with no references deletes right away; one that other documents rely on falls back to the base document instead; the base document itself is blocked while a strong reference still points at it.
steps.surface: variant delete confirmation dialog – reference check
surfaces: variant delete confirmation dialog – reference check
steps.screenCaption: delete confirmation dialog

flows.success: The desired variant document is gone. The editor feels confident about what has been deleted.
flows.failure: Deletion is blocked and the editor does not understand why, or variant documents remain hanging without a base.

painPoints.text: Before they delete, they cannot tell who stops seeing what, or whether they take the base document by accident.
The concept of a base document can be confusing. What happens when a base has been deleted?
A variant document that other documents rely on falls back to the base without anyone being told whose experience just changed.
Revert, delete, remove, reset. Testers could not tell the words apart.

flows.title: Delete a variant document with references

phases.title: Decide what to remove
phases.description: Open manage versions and choose what to remove.

phases.title: Confirm and resolve
phases.description: Confirm removal, and resolve what is still referenced.

flows.trigger: A content editor wants to remove several variant documents at once.

triggerMeta.screenCaption: the document editor, before touching version management

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They open manage versions from the document’s inventory.
steps.screenCaption: open manage versions from the inventory

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They select the variant documents to remove, across releases and perspectives.
steps.screenCaption: select variants across releases and perspectives

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: Variant documents with no references delete right away.
steps.screenCaption: unreferenced variants delete immediately

steps.label: STEP 4
steps.text: Variant documents still referenced are excluded instead, with a warning and a link to see what depends on them.
steps.surface: variant delete confirmation dialog – check what links here
surfaces: variant delete confirmation dialog – check what links here
steps.screenCaption: referenced variants are excluded, with a warning

steps.label: STEP 5
steps.text: From the warning, they open a dedicated view listing every reference, and unlink each one, hand it to the Content Agent, or move the referring document into a release for later.
steps.screenCaption: the unlink references panel

flows.success: The variant document deletes once nothing outside it still points at it.
flows.failure: The only way to find what’s blocking a deletion today is to leave the Studio and search for it by hand, so editors give up and leave the variant document in place.

painPoints.text: Publishing a new version can leave the old content with no references, and nobody notices.

quote.quote: “Once the new one published, that thing was not referenced anymore anywhere,”

tasks.title: Delete a variant definition
tasks.intro: A content editor retires a variant definition by finding out what still depends on it, and clearing that first.
tasks.desiredExperience: Retiring a definition is a guided cleanup, not a dead end. Editors see exactly what still depends on it and what to clear first, so removing it is a short, ordered checklist, not a wall they can't get past.

flows.title: Delete a variant definition that has no documents

phases.title: Decide what to retire
phases.description: Open the definition and check that it is empty.

phases.title: Confirm
phases.description: Confirm the permanent delete.

flows.trigger: A variant definition is no longer needed, and no variant documents use it.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They open the definition. Its list of variant documents is empty.
steps.screenCaption: the definition’s detail screen, with no variant documents

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They open its menu and choose Delete variant definition.
steps.screenCaption: its menu, with Delete variant definition

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They confirm. This permanently deletes the definition and cannot be undone.
steps.screenCaption: delete confirmation dialog

flows.success: The definition is removed.
flows.failure: They delete a definition they still needed, and nothing can bring it back.

flows.title: Delete a variant definition that still has variant documents

phases.title: Find what depends on it
phases.description: See which variant documents still use the definition.

phases.title: Clear and delete
phases.description: Remove its variant documents, then the definition.

flows.trigger: A variant definition is no longer needed, but variant documents still use it.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They open the definition and see the variant documents that still use it.
steps.screenCaption: the definition’s detail screen, listing its variant documents

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They open its menu. Delete is turned off, and a tooltip says the documents must be removed first.
steps.screenCaption: Delete turned off, with its tooltip

steps.label: STEP 3 · IDEA
steps.text: They open a view that lists every variant document using the definition, and delete them all in one go.
steps.surface: variant definition detail screen – remove documents view
surfaces: variant definition detail screen – remove documents view

steps.label: STEP 4
steps.text: With no documents left, they delete the definition and confirm.

flows.success: The definition and its variant documents are gone in one sitting.
flows.failure: They delete each variant document by hand, one at a time, and give up before the definition can go.

painPoints.text: Variant documents that still use the definition block its deletion, and each has to be cleared first.

tasks.title: Schedule and publish
tasks.intro: Variant documents are ready and have to go live now, at a moment, or together across many pages, and come down again after a set period. A release is how it is done together for a bunch of documents.
tasks.desiredExperience: Publishing feels coordinated, not scattered. Content for every audience goes live together at a known time, one switch turns a campaign on or off across every page it touches, and the editor can always see what's running and when it stops.

flows.title: Publish many together, via a release

phases.title: Bundle
phases.description: Put each variant document into the release when it is created.

phases.title: Publish many
phases.description: Find the release, review it, schedule or publish it.

flows.trigger: Variant documents across several base documents must go live at the same time.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: When creating each variant document, they set a release as its destination.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They open the Releases tool and find the release. They see all documents and variants that will be released together.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They review the documents in it and schedule it, or publish it now.

flows.success: Editors feel confident that all documents and variants in the release go live together at the chosen time.
flows.failure:
It’s cumbersome to verify whether the intended documents and their variants are ready to be released on a given date.

Orphaned variants are forgotten while the base document goes out to be released.

painPoints.text: Campaigns overlap, and the content editor has no timeline that shows which ones run at the same time.

quote.quote: “There could be some bumping into each other,”

painPoints.text: Publishing a new version through a release can leave the old content with no references, and nobody notices.

quote.quote: “Once the new one published, that thing was not referenced anymore anywhere,”

painPoints.text: To schedule a campaign that also switches itself off, they create two releases: one to publish it and one to revert it.
While a release waits, the pages above it are frozen too, so unrelated site-structure work has to wait with it.

quote.quote: “The release will lock everything parent above something that you’re changing,”

flows.title: Publish one variant document

phases.title: Publish one
phases.description: Put one variant document live.

flows.trigger: One variant document is done and should go live now.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: In the variant document, they choose Publish.

flows.success: The variant document is live; the audience gets it on the next request.
flows.failure: They publish believing the audience gets it on the next request, but a visitor keeps seeing the old content for a while after, and nobody can say how long the gap lasts.

flows.title: Take variant documents live for a limited time

phases.title: Schedule the start
phases.description: Put the changes in a release and schedule it.

phases.title: Schedule the end
phases.description: Build a second release that reverts them, and schedule it.

flows.trigger: Variant documents should go live for a set period, then go back to what was there before.

steps.label: STEP 1
steps.text: They put the changes into a release and schedule it for the start date.

steps.label: STEP 2
steps.text: They create a second release that reverts every one of those changes.

steps.label: STEP 3
steps.text: They schedule the second release for the end date.

steps.label: STEP 4 · IDEA
steps.text: They give the release an expiry date, so its changes revert on their own when it ends.

flows.success: The changes go live on the start date and are gone on the end date.
flows.failure: The reverting release misses a change, so part of it stays live after the end date and nobody notices.

painPoints.text: The content editor cannot set when a variant document starts and stops, so the team builds a custom document type with an end date.

quote.quote: “We built a special document type… with expiration date after the webinar ends,”

painPoints.text: Undoing a scheduled change takes a second release, built by hand to mirror the first.

quote.quote: “Still feels quite manual,”

painPoints.text: The site is built statically, so a campaign cannot start or end on time without webhooks.

quote.quote: “We’d need webhooks for campaign start/end,”

tasks.title: Measure
tasks.intro: Variant documents have been live for a while and the editor wants to know whether one performs better than another, or than the default. Nothing exists for this yet.
tasks.desiredExperience: Deciding what to keep feels evidence-based, not instinctive. The numbers on which variant document to keep, retire or promote line up with the analytics the team already reads, so the decision needs no separate translation step.

flows.title: Compare performance and decide

phases.title: Set up an experiment bundle
phases.description: Group the variant documents that one test covers.

phases.title: See how variant documents perform
phases.description: How the experiment bundle performed, as a set and per variant document.

phases.title: Decide
phases.description: Keep, retire, or promote a variant document to the default.

flows.trigger: The editor wants to know how one variant document performs against another.

steps.label: STEP 1 · IDEA
steps.text: They bundle the variant documents that serve one test, across several documents, into an experiment bundle, and start it.

steps.label: STEP 2 · IDEA
steps.text: They open the experiment bundle once it has run.

steps.label: STEP 3 · IDEA
steps.text: They see how the set performed, in views and conversion, against the default, and then each variant document within it.

steps.label: STEP 4 · IDEA
steps.text: They decide: keep, retire, or promote the experiment bundle’s variant documents to the default, together or one by one.

flows.success: Editors understand how the experiment bundle and each of its variant documents performed without leaving Sanity. The numbers come in from the team’s analytics tools, so they can decide and make edits with confidence, right where the content lives.
flows.failure: The numbers live in the analytics tool and have to be joined to variant documents by hand.

painPoints.text: The team cannot test which content works best, so someone picks one version for every visitor.

quote.quote: “They need to make a decision that this is the one piece of content that we’re going to provide, because we don’t have the luxury of actually optimizing what works. That’s my biggest problem,”

painPoints.text: Controlling the size of the audience is required before this can replace external tooling.

quote.quote: “Important feature… control the size of the audience,”

flows.title: A developer connects the analytics platform the team already uses

phases.title: Choose the source
phases.description: Decide which analytics platform the numbers come from, and what counts as success.

phases.title: Verify
phases.description: See the numbers appear against the variant documents in an experiment bundle.

flows.trigger: The team wants to measure variant documents in Sanity, and the developer needs to connect the platform where their numbers already live.

steps.label: STEP 1 · IDEA
steps.text: They choose the source: Google Analytics, another analytics or experimentation platform, a data warehouse, or any other endpoint where the team’s numbers live.

steps.label: STEP 2 · IDEA
steps.text: They tag the front end so every view reports which variant document it served.

steps.label: STEP 3 · IDEA
steps.text: They choose which metrics count as success, such as views and conversion, for each dataset.

steps.label: STEP 4 · IDEA
steps.text: They open an experiment bundle and check that the numbers appear against its variant documents.

flows.success: Numbers from the team’s own analytics arrive in Sanity, joined to the right variant documents, so editors read results without leaving the Studio.
flows.failure: Nothing reports which variant document was served, so the numbers cannot be joined back and the results stay in the analytics tool.

painPoints.text: Variant results do not match how the team already reports in Google Analytics.

quote.quote: “Align it to Google Analytics,”
